38.t: Why he came to Chicago: studying harmony at the Chicago Musical College
38.s: Levy came to study violin and harmony and wanted to know what the jazz players were doing.
38.q: I was studying the violin and I was interested in the piano and also in the harmony. And then when I heard some of those guys doing all this stuff, you know, as far as my classical training, I wanted to find out

50.t: What she knows of Jelly's schooling and where her information came from
50.s: She knows nothing of his education; her family information comes from an aunt by marriage, Viola Haynes.
50.ch: Family and early memories of Jelly
50.q: Well, I don't know anything about his education here, because, you see, I was the baby, and my grandmother never discussed anything with me. And all of this information that I'm giving you now, I got out of an aunt by marriage. My uncle's wife told me. My sister told me just a smidgen. She wouldn't…

741.t: Berklee: Herb Pomeroy and Jack Peterson
741.s: He credits the school atmosphere and two teachers, Pomeroy (arranging, workshops) and guitar teacher Jack Peterson.
741.q: Yeah I think so. I don’t know if I’d attribute it as much to the actual education that I got from specific teachers. I think it was more just the experience of being in school playing and developing and being around teachers and other students. And if anything I would attribute certain things of…

980.t: What Ellis Marsalis taught; music school versus gig experience
980.s: Caine learned from Marsalis through practical gig experience, went to Tulane one semester, and thinks jazz school can erode individuality.
980.q: Just that — I mean just gig experience you know? Just playing tunes you don’t know on the spot you know, and having to hear it, open up your ears and be able to hear your way through changes. I mean innumerable things. I only went to music school one semester with him so all of my, most of my…

437.t: Leaving a formal school and studying with Art Perretta
437.s: Unhappy at a formal school, he studies about three years with Art Perretta in Hartford, who gives classical training.
437.q: Yes I did. I went to a very formal school that we’ll just omit the name, and started to study there, and was not happy at all with the teaching staff and the direction I was going. Of course I had been out and playing, and I knew what I needed. I just wasn’t at their beck and call. I knew what I…

1020.t: A year back at Indiana University and George Gaber's lesson on touch
1020.s: Erskine left Kenton to return to school, where Gaber made him play a triangle softly to cure his heavy hitting.
1020.q: With a one year interruption. I left the road and decided to go back to school because I had dropped out of college to join the Kenton band. And it was an essential year of study and reflection, just trying to figure out what I was going to do next. I was in the odd position of being the one…

962.t: Music school versus self-taught guitar and voice
962.s: She is both self-taught (guitar, Gospel singing) and schooled, learning proper tuning and arranging for many band types.
962.q: That’s true. Yeah. I consider myself both. I was self taught when it came to guitar. I taught myself how to play guitar. But when I did go to school, to music school, I did learn the proper way to tune a guitar. I used to tune to an open G and I learned the proper way to tune a guitar when I went…

544.t: Studying with Konitz and Harold Danko
544.s: He did not quit college for music; he left Konitz when the lessons ran their course and studied piano and chord voicing for two years with Harold Danko, a fellow Youngstown native.
544.q: No. I didn’t have the guts. Plus I was, you know, this was my excuse for being in New York. So I mean I was studying with Konitz for a couple of years and then I started studying for a couple of years with Harold Danko, who by the way is also from Youngstown, Ohio, although I used to play outdoor…

585.t: Learning tunes and the Sydney Conservatorium
585.s: Bucky Pizzarelli's push for repertoire, her two years at the conservatorium with Mike Nock and Don Burrows, and the five Newcastle friends who became professionals.
585.q: Well, it’s funny, sometimes there’s two schools of thought in jazz. Bucky Pizzarelli, when he was at William Paterson, boy, I mean I knew some that studied with him, he really got on kids’ cases. I think Bucky can do it and get away with it, he’s just so wonderful. He’d get on kids’ cases about…

834.t: Ran Blake and the NEC jazz faculty
834.s: He studied a little with Ran Blake, preferring his own way, and describes faculty like Wilkins, Byard, McKinley, Giuffre and Russell as supportive.
834.q: A little bit with Ran Blake. I first went as a Third Stream major but I realized I got along with Ran a lot better if I was not in his program. Ran– you have to do it his way. Again, bless him, but I wanted to kind of do it my way. So their quote African American music or the jazz program was at…

503.t: Entering Wayne State and studying with Joe Fava
503.s: He chose Wayne for affordability, majored in theory and composition, and studied guitar technique with Joe Fava.
503.ch: High school, Dizzy and Wayne State
503.q: No, its just one I could afford, because we still didn’t have much money. But it was a good school and so I applied as a freshman and I wanted to major in music and the concentration was theory and composition.

110.t: Unable to read: the promise never to teach
110.s: He dodged keyboard requirements, was nearly refused graduation, and was saved by his harmony and counterpoint teachers on condition he never teach.
110.ch: Stockton, Pacific and the Army years
110.q: It was worse than that. I avoided the conservatory, knowing I couldn’t read, by – there were certain requirements that you had to do. You had to play other instruments: brass or windwind or string. Finally, you had to pass basic keyboard. I avoided that by taking clarinet. You were usually just…

134.t: Choral playing and hymn harmony with Dyett
134.s: He praises Dyett's training in four-part hymns and spirituals as the best lesson in harmony.
134.q: Just music in general. It’s good for piano players and everybody. It’s three- and four-note harmony – two-, three-, four-note harmony.

64.t: Harmony and theory with Henry Grant and Mary Europe at Dunbar High School
64.s: Grant and Mary Europe taught instrumental and vocal music with strict attention to harmony; Duke Ellington respected Grant.
64.q: Yes. I was… with Henry Grant and with other music teachers… Mary Riece Europe was one our teachers, this is Jim Europe’s sister… taught at Dunbar High School. She and Henry Grant were personally responsible for many of the great artists

528.t: Theory and harmony at the Granoff School
528.s: He studied theory and harmony at Granoff on his own initiative to explore harmony beyond his piano teacher's European classics.
528.ch: Cal Massey, Coltrane and the Jazztet
528.q: Yes, on my own because my piano teacher taught me some more of the European classics, books and thing, but that was a good way for me to explore things harmonically and deal with it in that way. Then when Bud Powell moved into the neighborhood that was wonderful. One of my heroes moving in the…

137.t: The Chicago trade school and learning from Don Redman in New York
137.s: He lived with Dr. Dorsey, worked at the lunch counter, learned musical terms at school, then in New York met Bingie Madison and Don Redman's six-part harmony.
137.ch: Circus shows and learning to voice
137.q: Yeah, I went there, because my brother knew a doctor there named Dr. Dorsey, and I lived with Dr. Dorsey, he owned a drugstore. And then from -- I worked a little at the lunch counter and I would go down to this trade school. You'd work your way through it, and I worked in the bakery shop for…

614.t: College-trained players and Alan Broadbent's recommendation
614.s: Music schools, especially in Boston, began supplying technically strong players; Nat Pierce and George Shearing recommended Broadbent.
614.q: Well, that was the beginning, actually. The music schools were starting to give us new guys that we'd never seen the likes of before, because they could do things that, really, we hadn't even attempted yet. By that I mean their technical proficiency and the things we could attempt now were a little…

387.t: Studying with Gruenberg, Howard Murphy and Wagner
387.s: Chicago Musical College study in 1937, then Teachers College and private work with Bernard Wagner.
387.q: What is involved is not so much a lifting, but a spark, a stimulation. If they were bored with it, they wouldn't listen to it. I think they were stimulated by it, as I was, which caused me to go and study with a guy named Louis Gruenberg while we were at the Black Hawk in Chicago. This was at the…

19.t: WPA band as professional training: daily rehearsal and harmony class
19.s: Rehearsing every day with a government-paid harmony teacher became his real training.
19.ch: U Street, Jelly Roll Morton, the youth band and the WPA
19.q: I wrote a lot of music with that band, and I played with some excellent musicians. I played a lot of different kind of music, and I think that's where I got my real professional training as a musician.

75.t: Self-taught musicians and New York as the mecca
75.s: He reflects on being self-taught, cutting school to hear pianists who came to New York from everywhere.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: : Well, (?) was self-taught to a degree. My education in music came further along the line, after I fished around a lot, you know. Then later on, when I began making a conscious effort into my music...or attention, you know...

78.t: What school gave him versus learning in New York
78.s: School gave a foundation, but his real education came from asking the giants of jazz in New York, including the jam sessions at Coleman Hawkins' place.
78.ch: Learning from Fletcher's circle in New York
78.q: It did give me the foundation, Tom, a little bit, you know, but my greatest experience came from being in New York, seeing these giants of jazz execute it, and being able to ask them questions and them givin' me the correct answer. There weren't too many books out, as you know, during that time…
